proof.command: read packages/envoy/infra/gcp/dispatch_kube.go:290-305 and packages/envoy/infra/gcp/dispatch_test.go:505-520; compare with kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle, Pod termination
proof.observed: Both now say the control plane takes the pod out of its EndpointSlice as soon as the deletion timestamp appears, concurrently with the kubelet beginning graceful termination — the hook first, SIGTERM once it returns — and that the removal then has to reach every node's proxy and Tailscale Serve, so the sleep runs alongside the propagation and is sized to outlast it. That is what the documentation says: 'At the same time as the kubelet is starting graceful shutdown of the Pod, the control plane evaluates whether to remove that shutting-down Pod from EndpointSlice objects', with the hook run before the TERM signal. The README sentence corrected in round 4 agrees with both.

unproven: Unchanged and still INFRA-63's, since no pod in Legion reaches a cluster or the consuming stack's state: Tailscale Serve resolving the app's cluster DNS name under TS_USERSPACE=true; the cutover's two tailscaled processes against one state Secret, with the consuming program still minting the tailnet key Reusable: false; the front door's unmeasured 100m/128Mi reservation; and whether a release loses no request — which is the measurement that decides whether five seconds of pre-stop wait outlasts the propagation it now correctly runs alongside.

The reviewer's own minor stands: 35 s is a floor rather than a cover, since the kubelet charges the hook's elapsed time — the sleep plus the CRI exec overhead — against the one grace period, leaving envoy-dispatch a little under 30 s. The design's five-second reserve absorbs it and the tightest pinned case is the 27 s lock; nothing here measures the overhead.
observations: The deletion left the coupling better held than before, not merely smaller: the surviving pair assertion pins what the component renders, the golden pins it byte for byte, and the one inequality lives on the side that can read stopGrace rather than copy it. The control that lowers the component's grace and regenerates the golden fails on both sides, which is the shape a reader should expect — the renderer's tests catch the rendering, the server's test catches the relation.
